```{r}
#| label: setup
source("functions.R")
pop <- populations$normal
```

# 1. What population are you sampling from?

I start with the standard normal population: mean 0, standard deviation 1, skewness 0 and excess kurtosis 0.
I treat this as my control experiment. The mean of independent normal observations is exactly normal for every n,
so I already know the right answer before simulating. Anything that looks "non normal" here can only come from
Monte Carlo noise, which makes this the place to check that my standard for "normal enough" does not reject a
distribution that is truly normal.

```{r}
#| label: population
set.seed(student_id)
popDraws <- pop$generator(100000)

hist(popDraws, breaks = 60, probability = TRUE, col = "gray85", border = "white",
     main = "Population: 100,000 draws from N(0, 1)", xlab = "Individual value")
curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)

data.frame(
  quantity    = c("mean", "sd", "skewness", "excess kurtosis"),
  theoretical = c(pop$mu, pop$sigma, pop$gamma1, pop$gamma2),
  simulated   = c(mean(popDraws), sd(popDraws), skewness(popDraws), exKurtosis(popDraws))
)
```

The simulated population values match the theoretical ones closely, so the generator behaves as expected.

The assignment uses N(0, 1), but I wanted to know whether the choice of mean and standard deviation matters for
the shape results. I reran the full experiment with three other normal populations, using the same seed.

```{r}
#| label: meanSdCheck
meanSd <- data.frame(mu = c(0, 100, -5, 0), sigma = c(1, 15, 0.1, 50))
shapeRuns <- lapply(1:nrow(meanSd), function(i) {
  p <- pop
  m <- meanSd$mu[i]; s <- meanSd$sigma[i]
  p$generator <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = m, sd = s)
  p$mu <- m; p$sigma <- s
  analyzePopulation(p)$table
})
meanSd$chosenN <- sapply(shapeRuns, smallestN)
meanSd$maxSkew <- sapply(shapeRuns, function(t) max(abs(t$skew)))
meanSd$minQQ   <- sapply(shapeRuns, function(t) min(t$qqCor))
meanSd$minSE   <- sapply(shapeRuns, function(t) min(t$seRatio))
knitr::kable(meanSd, digits = 4)
```

Every row gives the same chosen n, skewness, QQ correlation and SE ratio. Shifting a normal distribution or
stretching it changes where the sample means sit and how spread out they are, but not their shape, and my
diagnostics only measure shape and the ratio to sigma / sqrt(n). So one experiment with N(0, 1) covers every
normal population.

# 2. What did you expect before running the simulation?

For iid data the skewness of the sample mean is gamma1 / sqrt(n) and the excess kurtosis is gamma2 / n.
Both are 0 here, and a sum of independent normal variables is itself normal, so I expected the sampling
distribution to be normal already at n = 1.

```{r}
#| label: prediction
predictedN(pop$gamma1)
```

Since the answer is known, the real question for this file is how much my diagnostics move by chance alone.
With num repetitions, the skewness estimate from truly normal data has a standard error of about
sqrt(6 / num) and the excess kurtosis about sqrt(24 / num). For the value I use in the main analysis
(num = `r format(num, big.mark = ",")`):

```{r}
#| label: noise
c(skewNoiseSE = sqrt(6 / num), kurtNoiseSE = sqrt(24 / num))
```

My cutoffs (|skewness| at most `r criteria$skew`, |excess kurtosis| at most `r criteria$kurt`) are about
`r round(criteria$skew / sqrt(6 / num))` and `r round(criteria$kurt / sqrt(24 / num))` times larger than this noise,
so I predicted that a truly normal sampling distribution would pass at every n.

# 3. Which sample sizes did you investigate?

## Choosing the number of repetitions (num)

n and num are different things: n is the size of one sample, and num is how many samples I simulate to see the
sampling distribution. Changing num does not change the true sampling distribution, only how precisely I can
measure it. Before fixing num, I ran the whole normal experiment with four values. Since the population is exactly
normal, every n should pass; any failure here would be caused by too few repetitions, not by the CLT.

```{r}
#| label: numCompare
numValues <- c(100, 1000, 10000, 100000)
numCompare <- do.call(rbind, lapply(numValues, function(k) {
  seconds <- system.time(t <- analyzePopulation(pop, reps = k)$table)["elapsed"]
  data.frame(num = k,
             passed = sum(t$normalEnough), tested = nrow(t),
             maxSkew = max(abs(t$skew)), maxKurt = max(abs(t$exKurt)),
             minQQ = min(t$qqCor),
             minSE = min(t$seRatio), maxSE = max(t$seRatio), seOK = sum(t$seOK),
             skewNoise = sqrt(6 / k),
             seconds = unname(seconds))
}))
knitr::kable(transform(numCompare, num = format(num, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)), digits = 4)
nc <- function(k, column) numCompare[numCompare$num == k, column]
```

To see what num changes, I drew the n = 30 sampling distribution from each run. These are the same simulated
means that produced the n = 30 rows of the table above.

```{r}
#| label: numPlot
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 3.5
numMeans <- lapply(numValues, function(k) {
  set.seed(student_id)
  simMeans(pop$generator, 30, reps = k)
})
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, length(numValues)), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (i in 1:length(numValues)) {
  hist(numMeans[[i]], breaks = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.05), probability = TRUE, col = "gray85", border = "white",
       xlim = c(-0.7, 0.7), ylim = c(0, 3),
       main = paste("num =", format(numValues[i], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)), xlab = "Sample mean (n = 30)")
  curve(dnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = 1 / sqrt(30)), add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
}
par(old)
```

Putting the four runs on one plot makes the comparison easier. Each line connects the bar heights of a histogram
with bins 0.1 wide.

```{r}
#| label: numOverlay
#| fig.width: 9
#| fig.height: 5
numCols <- c("darkorange", "seagreen", "steelblue", "purple")
numLty  <- c(1, 1, 1, 2)
xs <- seq(-0.6, 0.6, length.out = 400)
plot(xs, dnorm(xs, mean = 0, sd = 1 / sqrt(30)), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "black",
     ylim = c(0, 3), xlab = "Sample mean (n = 30)", ylab = "Density",
     main = "Same n = 30, different num: how well the simulation traces the true curve")
for (i in 1:length(numValues)) {
  m <- numMeans[[i]]
  h <- hist(m, breaks = seq(floor(min(m) * 10) / 10, ceiling(max(m) * 10) / 10, by = 0.1), plot = FALSE)
  lines(h$mids, h$density, type = "o", pch = 16, col = numCols[i], lwd = 2, lty = numLty[i])
}
legend("topright",
       c("True curve (theory)", paste("num =", trimws(format(numValues, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)))),
       col = c("black", numCols), lwd = c(3, 2, 2, 2, 2), lty = c(1, numLty), pch = c(NA, 16, 16, 16, 16), bty = "n")
```

The true curve (red in the panels, black in the combined plot) is the same for every num, because n did not change: the true sampling distribution of the mean
of 30 normal values is always N(0, 1 / sqrt(30)). The only difference is how closely the bars trace that curve.
With 100 means the bars are jagged and some bins are empty; with 100,000 they follow the curve almost exactly.

With num = 100, `r nc(100, "passed")` of `r nc(100, "tested")` sample sizes passed my standard, even though the
population is exactly normal. The skewness noise at num = 100 is about `r round(nc(100, "skewNoise"), 3)`, which is
larger than my cutoff of `r criteria$skew`, so the measurement is too noisy for the standard I set.

With num = 1,000, `r nc(1000, "passed")` of `r nc(1000, "tested")` passed, but the evidence is weaker than it looks: the
largest |skewness| was `r round(nc(1000, "maxSkew"), 3)` (close to my cutoff of `r criteria$skew`), and the SE ratio ranged
from `r round(nc(1000, "minSE"), 3)` to `r round(nc(1000, "maxSE"), 3)`, so only `r nc(1000, "seOK")` of `r nc(1000, "tested")` sample sizes passed
my 5 percent SE check. That failure comes from noise in the simulated SD, not from the formula sigma / sqrt(n).

With num = 10,000 the largest |skewness| dropped to `r round(nc(10000, "maxSkew"), 3)`, and with num = 100,000 to
`r round(nc(100000, "maxSkew"), 3)`. Both pass every n and every SE check, so the extra precision of 100,000 does not
change any decision, while it took about `r round(nc(100000, "seconds") / nc(10000, "seconds"))` times longer to run.

I chose num = 10,000 for the main analysis: it is the smallest of the values I tried where my cutoffs sit well above
the noise, and it keeps the rendering time short. (The seconds column depends on the computer and changes from run to run.)

## Sample sizes

I used the grid `r paste(pop$coarse, collapse = ", ")`. I included very small values (1, 2, 3) on purpose,
because if the theory is right the small n cases should already look normal, and that is where a problem with my
criteria would show up first. I did not expect to need a finer grid.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
res <- analyzePopulation(pop)
tab <- res$table
nStar <- smallestN(tab)
showTable(tab)
```

## Choosing my cutoffs

My cutoffs also needed testing. A cutoff that is too strict will reject a truly normal distribution just because of
Monte Carlo noise, so I tried several values for each check on the table above and counted how many of the
`r nrow(tab)` sample sizes passed. Each column uses only that one check.

```{r}
#| label: cutoffCompare
skewCuts <- c(0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3)
kurtCuts <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5)
seCuts   <- c(0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.1)
cutCompare <- data.frame(
  skewCut = skewCuts, skewPassed = sapply(skewCuts, function(k) sum(abs(tab$skew) <= k)),
  kurtCut = kurtCuts, kurtPassed = sapply(kurtCuts, function(k) sum(abs(tab$exKurt) <= k)),
  seTol   = seCuts,   sePassed   = sapply(seCuts,   function(k) sum(abs(tab$seRatio - 1) <= k))
)
knitr::kable(cutCompare)
skewFloor <- min(skewCuts[cutCompare$skewPassed == nrow(tab)])
kurtFloor <- min(kurtCuts[cutCompare$kurtPassed == nrow(tab)])
seFloor   <- min(seCuts[cutCompare$sePassed == nrow(tab)])
```

For skewness, a cutoff of `r skewCuts[1]` accepted only `r cutCompare$skewPassed[1]` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes,
and the smallest cutoff I tried that accepted all of them was `r skewFloor`. For kurtosis the smallest such cutoff was
`r kurtFloor`, and for the SE check it was `r seFloor * 100` percent.

I did not pick those smallest values. They only just pass on this seed, and with a different seed the noise could
push a truly normal distribution over them. I chose skewness `r criteria$skew`, kurtosis `r criteria$kurt` and
SE tolerance `r seTol * 100` percent, which leave a clear margin above the noise
(`r round(criteria$skew / skewFloor, 1)`, `r round(criteria$kurt / kurtFloor, 1)` and `r round(seTol / seFloor, 1)` times the smallest
passing values). Whether these cutoffs are strict enough to catch a real departure from normality cannot be
tested here, because the normal population has none. I check that with the exponential population in 03exponential.qmd.

```{r}
#| label: summaryNumbers
maxSkew   <- max(abs(tab$skew))
maxKurt   <- max(abs(tab$exKurt))
minQQ     <- min(tab$qqCor)
seRange   <- range(tab$seRatio)
tailRange <- range(c(tab$tailLow, tab$tailHigh))
nReject   <- sum(tab$swP < 0.05)
meanGapZ  <- abs(tab$simMean - tab$theoMean) / (tab$theoSE / sqrt(num))
```

# 4. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{n = `r nStar`}$$

`r sum(tab$normalEnough)` of the `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes I tested met my standard.

# 5. How do the simulated mean and standard error compare with theory?

The CLT makes three claims about the sample mean: its center is mu, its spread is sigma / sqrt(n), and its shape becomes
normal. This section checks the first two; section 6 checks the shape.

```{r}
#| label: seCheck
tab[, c("n", "simMean", "theoMean", "simSD", "theoSE", "seRatio", "seOK")]
```

```{r}
#| label: sePlot
plotSE(tab, label = "Normal")
```

Center: the simulated mean of the sample means was never more than `r round(max(abs(tab$simMean - tab$theoMean)), 4)` away
from mu = 0. The simulated mean itself has Monte Carlo error of about (theoretical SE) / sqrt(num), and the largest gap
was `r round(max(meanGapZ), 2)` of those Monte Carlo standard errors, which is consistent with random noise.

Spread: the simulated SD of the means divided by sigma / sqrt(n) stayed between `r round(seRange[1], 3)` and
`r round(seRange[2], 3)`, and `r sum(tab$seOK)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes passed my 5 percent SE check. On the log scale plot the
simulated points sit on the theoretical line, which falls with slope minus one half: multiplying n by 4 halves the SE.

# 6. Why did you choose that value?

```{r}
#| label: samplingPlots
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 6
plotSampling(res, nShow = c(1, 5, 30, 100), mu = pop$mu, theoSE = iidSE(pop$sigma), label = pop$label)
```

In every histogram the red curve (the CLT prediction) and the blue dashed curve (a normal curve with the simulated
mean and SD) lie on top of each other and follow the bars. The QQ plots are straight lines from end to end, with no
curve in the middle (which would mean skew) and no bending at the ends (which would mean heavy or light tails).

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4
plotConvergence(tab, label = "Normal")
```

Unlike the other populations, there is no downward trend here: skewness and kurtosis just scatter around 0 at
every n, which is what pure noise should look like.

I chose n = `r nStar` because every piece of shape evidence agrees, starting at the smallest sample size I tested:

* The largest |skewness| across all n was `r round(maxSkew, 3)` and the largest |excess kurtosis| was
  `r round(maxKurt, 3)`. Both are within a few noise standard errors of 0 and below my cutoffs.
* The QQ correlation never dropped below `r round(minQQ, 4)`, compared with my cutoff of `r criteria$qqCor`.
* The share of sample means beyond ±1.96 standard deviations stayed between `r round(tailRange[1], 4)` and
  `r round(tailRange[2], 4)` in each tail, close to the 0.025 a normal distribution gives.

This result is mostly a check on my method. Since my standard accepts a distribution I know is normal at every n,
I can trust that when it rejects another population later, the rejection reflects a real departure from normality
and not just Monte Carlo noise.

# 7. What surprised you?

The biggest surprise was the num experiment in section 3. With num = 100, my standard rejected an exactly normal
population at `r nc(100, "tested") - nc(100, "passed")` of `r nc(100, "tested")` sample sizes. Nothing about the population or the CLT changed
between num = 100 and num = 10,000; only the number of simulated samples did. A "not normal" verdict can therefore be
a statement about my simulation rather than about the data, which is why I fixed num before choosing any n.

I also checked the Shapiro Wilk test, which I report but do not use for my decision:

```{r}
#| label: shapiroCheck
tab[, c("n", "swW", "swP")]
nReject
```

It gave p < 0.05 at `r nReject` of the `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes (smallest p value `r signif(min(tab$swP), 2)` at
n = `r tab$n[which.min(tab$swP)]`). Because the population is exactly normal, any rejection here would be a false alarm;
at the 5 percent level the test is expected to reject a true null about 1 time in 20. My rows are also not independent
of each other (I reset the seed before each n, so they reuse the same random stream), so one unlucky stream could
affect several rows at once.
